Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Agentic process evidence
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: UPPAAi: Towards LLM-Assisted Modeling, Verification, Analysis and Synthesis
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: For more than three decades, UPPAAL has supported the modelling and analysis of real-time and cyber-physical systems. Yet building a suitable model, formalising the intended properties, choosing analysis techniques and interpreting counterexamples remain iterative tasks that demand substantial expertise. Large language models (LLMs) can offer plausible explanations and even solutions, but they are not necessarily correct. We present UPPAAI, an extension of UPPAAL in which users construct, explain, debug and specify models in dialogue with an LLM. The guiding principle is that the user requests, the LLM proposes, explains and orchestrates, and UPPAAL verifies. UPPAAI exposes the UPPAAL editor, queries and verifier through a Tools API. We report on seven case studies, from explaining to a newcomer to learning a controller, covering timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata and strategy learning. LLMs proved to be extremely helpful in not just generating solutions but also pro-actively suggesting relevant UPPAAL features it was not asked about.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Red Teaming Program Repair Agents: When Correct Patches can Hide Vulnerabilities
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed for software maintenance tasks such as automated program repair (APR). APR agents automatically fetch GitHub issues and use backend LLMs to generate patches that fix the reported bugs. However, existing work primarily focuses on the functional correctness of APR-generated patches, whether they pass hidden or regression tests, while largely ignoring potential security risks. Given the openness of platforms like GitHub, where any user can raise issues and participate in discussions, an important question arises: Can an adversarial user submit a valid issue on GitHub that misleads an LLM-based agent into generating a functionally correct but vulnerable patch? To answer this question, we propose SWExploit, which generates adversarial issue statements designed to make APR agents produce patches that are functionally correct yet vulnerable. SWExploit operates in three main steps: (1) program analysis to identify potential injection points for vulnerable payloads; (2) adversarial issue generation to provide misleading reproduction and error information while preserving the original issue semantics; and (3) iterative refinement of the adversarial issue statements based on the outputs of the APR agents. Empirical evaluation on three agent pipelines and five backend LLMs shows that SWExploit can produce patches that are both functionally correct and vulnerable (the attack success rate on the correct patch could reach 0.91, whereas the baseline ASRs are all below 0.20). Based on our evaluation, we are the first to challenge the traditional assumption that a patch passing all tests is inherently reliable and secure, highlighting critical limitations in the current evaluation paradigm for APR agents.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: This paper is accepted to COLM 2026

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: ExploreRepair: Evidence-Specialized Agents for Vulnerability Repair under Information Constraints
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Automated vulnerability repair must often operate with incomplete vulnerability information: developers may lack an accurate vulnerability classification or a provided proof-of-vulnerability (PoV) test, yet still need to produce a repair. Without detailed information, a key challenge is to explore multiple plausible interpretations of the vulnerability before committing to a repair. To address this challenge, we propose ExploreRepair, a vulnerability repair framework that reconciles the vulnerability observations and repair implementations from a team of exploration agents. We first collect these observations and repair implementations from three agents, each tasked with exploring a specific dimension of the vulnerability. Then, a Lesson Aggregator and a Patch Aggregator independently synthesize repairs from these observations and concrete implementations before a final Aggregator reconciles their proposals without benchmark feedback. On PatchEval, ExploreRepair achieves repair success rates of 39.6% and 71.6% with GPT-5.6-Luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, exceeding EvoRepair, a state-of-the-art vulnerability repair approach, by 16.0 and 25.4 percentage points. On VulnLoc+, it achieves success rates of 51.4% and 62.9%, respectively, exceeding LoopRepair's variant without PoV tests by 20.0 and 17.1 percentage points.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: PR4Code: A Pull Requests Dataset for AI Code Generation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI-driven code generation is evolving from handling small, localized code-completion tasks toward supporting the implementation of full software features. To support this transition, this paper introduces PR4Code, a dataset of 4,508 Java and 8,831 Python curated Pull Requests (PRs) collected from GitHub, each enriched with metadata, commit histories, and detailed code changes. Unlike resources focused on isolated code fragments, PR4Code captures the feature implementation process, delivering a large and diverse collection of real-world development tasks that can be used to assess AI-driven solutions. Our analysis reveals substantial variability in PR structure, commit granularity, and textual content. In addition, we release scripts to regenerate and update the dataset, ensuring reproducibility and maintainability.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: STORY2DIFF: A Dataset Linking Real-World User Stories to Code Changes
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Research on requirements-to-code tasks needs examples in which a genuine requirement is paired with the change that implemented it. Existing user-story collections, however, largely contain isolated or synthetic text. To address this limitation, we present STORY2DIFF, a dataset of 7,785 English user stories linked to merged pull requests from January 2017 to July 2026. The dataset is mined from a set of 982 public Java and Python repositories. Each record in the dataset combines the original issue, extracted Connextra elements, the associated pull request and commit metadata, a file-level diff capturing the code changes introduced by the associated pull request, and the affected files before and after the change. The tool we built to mine STORY2DIFF can be used to repeat the automatic extraction of the records, using different parameters (e.g., a different timeframe). The dataset can support a variety of tasks, including requirement discovery, traceability, change- impact estimation, and requirements-aware code generation. Dataset: https://github.com/riganelli/user-story-mining-pipeline/ releases/tag/V4.0.1. Video: https://youtu.be/qOhXUeyeiTQ.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Submitted to the ICSE 2027 Demonstrations and Data Showcase track

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: From Conversation to Evaluation: Benchmarking LLMs on Development Knowledge via SimpleDevQA
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The Development Knowledge Question Answering (Dev Knowledge QA) task aims to provide accurate natural language answers to knowledge-seeking questions during software development. To investigate the importance of Dev Knowledge QA in AI-assisted software development and the extent to which it has been explored, we conduct a preliminary analysis of real user-LLM dialogues from WildChat. Our findings indicate that Dev Knowledge QA plays a significant role in real-world software development scenarios, and these raw dialogues cannot be directly used to construct a Dev Knowledge QA benchmark. Existing Dev Knowledge QA benchmarks are limited in development knowledge scope and often not built from real user queries. To bridge this gap, we design a three-phase pipeline that transforms real-world dialogue into simple development knowledge-seeking QA pairs. Through this pipeline, we introduce SimpleDevQA, a multilingual Dev Knowledge QA benchmark inspired by real user dialogues. This dataset covers three languages (English, Chinese, and Russian), and focuses on questions with unique, short, and verifiable answers, making evaluation more accurate and simple. Extensive experiments with 21 mainstream LLMs show that closed-source models generally perform best on SimpleDevQA. We also find that RAG-based knowledge injection improves accuracy, and that Dev Knowledge QA performance correlates with both model confidence and code-generation capability. To facilitate the replication study, we have released our data and code at: https://github.com/DeepSoftwareAnalytics/SimpleDevQA.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Latent Anchor-Driven Test Generation for Deep Neural Networks
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are increasingly being deployed in security-critical and safety-sensitive applications, which makes rigorous testing essential to identify and mitigate model weaknesses. Existing DNN testing approaches explore either the input space or a learned latent space. While latent-space generation can better maintain plausibility than direct input-space mutation, current methods still face a trade-off among exploration controllability, failure diversity, and seed-relative semantic drift. To overcome these limitations, we propose Latte, a black-box testing framework that generates semantically proximate, diverse, and fault-revealing test cases by leveraging the latent space. Specifically, Latte encodes each input seed with a pre-trained VQ-VAE and performs a seed-centered, one-step latent mutation along directions defined by anchors sampled from alternative classes, followed by quantization and decoding back to the input space. This explores local neighborhoods around each seed within the learned latent manifold, resulting in a larger number and broader diversity of oracle-triggering prediction discrepancies under the same budget. We evaluated Latte on 5 datasets and 10 DNN models in single-model and multi-model testing scenarios. Across the evaluated datasets and models, Latte improves fault exposure and behavioral diversity under matched testing budgets. Under the single-model setting, it also maintains low seed-relative semantic drift with respect to the source seeds.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Testing Deep Learning Library APIs via Cross-Framework Differential Fuzzing
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Deep learning libraries underpin many safety- and reliability-critical applications, yet existing API-level testing techniques often rely on intra-library properties or CPU--GPU differential oracles and may miss defects that behave consistently across hardware backends. We present Xamt, a cross-framework differential fuzzing approach for deep learning library APIs. Xamt constructs and tests execution-validated groups of APIs intended to implement equivalent operations across seven libraries. It uses explicit API aliases and parameter-role normalization to construct candidate correspondences and validates them through pairwise execution and a group-level behavioral check on canonical ordinary inputs. The resulting groups are explored using variance-guided differential fuzzing with ordinary, boundary, and non-finite inputs. Crash and inconsistency oracles flag executions exhibiting abnormal termination or inconsistent outputs for subsequent reproduction and analysis. Across the seven libraries, Xamt constructs 676 execution-validated groups containing 2,563 matched APIs. Among these, Xamt identifies 72 independently reproduced discrepancy cases, including 4 crash cases and 68 output inconsistencies. Among the 72 developer reports, 25 have been confirmed, including 23 that have been fixed.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Early Prediction of Cross-Service Implementation Scope: Evidence and Limits from Multiple Microservice Projects
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Microservice architectures aim to localize change, yet feature requests may require implementation across service boundaries. We investigate how well such downstream scope can be anticipated before implementation begins. Using issue--pull-request--commit traceability and implementation evidence corrected through targeted human adjudication, we reconstruct 866 repository-traceable feature requests from 13 open-source microservice projects and map their implementations to validated service boundaries. Cross-service changes occur in 101 requests (11.7%) and exhibit broader implementation footprints, particularly higher code churn, but no clear difference in lead time. Pre-implementation evidence provides limited cross-project predictive signal: the strongest leave-one-system-out model reaches a project-macro Macro-F1 of 0.484, but its advantage over the majority baseline is not significant after Holm correction and is sensitive to small evaluation folds. A local LLM offers no reliable improvement over classical models. Downstream workload is substantially harder to estimate, as learned models do not consistently outperform training-fold median baselines. A simple service-mention heuristic also performs comparably to learned scope triage. These findings show that early feature-request evidence is more useful for lightweight cross-service scope triage than for automated scope determination or precise workload estimation.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: zkCraft: Prompt-Guided LLM as a Zero-Shot Mutation Pattern Oracle for TCCT-Powered ZK Fuzzing
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Zero-knowledge circuits enable privacy-preserving and scalable systems but are difficult to implement correctly due to the tight coupling between witness computation and circuit constraints. We present zkCraft, a practical framework that combines deterministic, R1CS-aware localization with proof-bearing search to detect semantic inconsistencies. zkCraft encodes candidate constraint edits into a single Row-Vortex polynomial and replaces repeated solver queries with a Violation IOP that certifies the existence of edits together with a succinct proof. Deterministic LLM-driven mutation templates bias exploration toward edge cases while preserving auditable algebraic verification. Evaluation on real Circom code shows that proof-bearing localization detects diverse under- and over-constrained faults with low false positives and reduces costly solver interaction. Our approach bridges formal verification and automated debugging, offering a scalable path for robust ZK circuit development.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: CodeArena: A Collective Evaluation Platform for LLM Code Generation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have reshaped code generation by synergizing their exceptional comprehension of natural language and programming syntax, thereby substantially boosting developer productivity. These advancements have prompted numerous efforts to quantitatively evaluate their coding capabilities. However, persistent challenges, such as benchmark leakage, data dissipation, and limited system accessibility, continue to impede a timely and accurate assessment. To address these limitations, we introduce CodeArena, an online evaluation framework tailored for LLM code generation. The key innovation is a collective evaluation mechanism, which dynamically recalibrates individual model scores based on the holistic performance of all participating models, mitigating score biases caused by widespread benchmark leakage. In addition, CodeArena ensures open access to all submitted solutions and test cases and provides automation-friendly APIs to streamline the code evaluation workflow. Our main contributions are: (1) a collective evaluation system for unbiased assessment, (2) a public repository of solutions and test cases, and (3) automation-ready APIs for seamless integration.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: FuzzAgent: Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Evolutionary Library Fuzzing
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Library fuzzing synthesizes harnesses that expose new API interactions, but deploying it end to end still requires extensive project-specific integration. Existing LLM-based systems automate individual steps, yet they treat execution outcomes as coarse signals: a stalled campaign does not reveal which state blocks progress, and a crash trace does not reveal whether the library or the harness is at fault. We present FuzzAgent, a multi-agent system that builds and evolves a complete fuzzing campaign from a source tree alone. Specialized agents acquire project knowledge and repair campaign artifacts automatically. Hierarchical coverage diagnosis localizes blockers from modules down to branches, and dependency-aware generation converts them into harnesses with the required API lifecycle. Crash validation recovers runtime object states to distinguish harness misuse from library bugs.
  We evaluate FuzzAgent on 20 real-world C/C++ libraries against five state-of-the-art baselines (OSS-Fuzz, OSS-Fuzz-Gen, PromptFuzz, PromeFuzz, and ProteusFuzz). FuzzAgent completes the full fuzzing lifecycle for all 20 libraries without human intervention at $3.17 per library. On the 20 libraries, it reaches 179619 branches, exceeding OSS-Fuzz, PromptFuzz, ProteusFuzz, PromeFuzz, and OSS-Fuzz-Gen by 45.1%, 73.2%, 87.7%, 92.1%, and 191.2%, respectively. FuzzAgent also identifies 102 new library bugs, 90 of which have already been acknowledged or fixed by upstream maintainers.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Lost in the Latent Space: How Code Embeddings Represent Functional Intent and Implementation Fidelity
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Code embedding models have become a key building block for many software engineering applications, yet their internal representations remain poorly understood. Existing evaluations tend to focus on downstream task performance, offering limited insight into whether a single embedding can support both functional abstraction and implementation-sensitive analysis. To address this gap, we present a large-scale empirical study of 14 state-of-the-art code embedding models. We evaluate their representational behavior through three complementary analyses: supervised probing for functional abstraction and implementation fidelity, zero-shot retrieval experiments to assess geometric similarity, and controlled perturbation experiments that measure embedding responses to semantics-preserving code transformations. The results reveal a consistent abstraction-fidelity tension: models that better preserve stylistic and structural signals tend to do so at the expense of semantic generalization, while models with similar retrieval performance can nevertheless respond very differently to the same implementation changes. Overall, our findings suggest that a single universal code representation remains out of reach, motivating more representation-aware evaluation, selection, and deployment of code embedding models in software engineering.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: BlueCodeAgent: A Blue Teaming Agent Powered by Automated Red Teaming for CodeGen AI
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Existing research on CodeGen AI security mainly focuses on red teaming, which aims to uncover vulnerabilities and risks in AI-generated code. However, progress on the blue teaming side remains limited, as effective defenses require a deep security analysis of given tasks and edge cases. To fill in this gap, we propose BlueCodeAgent, an end-to-end blue teaming agent powered by automated red teaming. Our red teaming component generates diverse risky instances, providing effective edge cases and guidance for the subsequent blue teaming process. Our blue teaming agent then conducts multi-level defense, leveraging these red teaming examples to detect previously seen and unseen risk scenarios through constitution summarization and dynamic code analysis. Our evaluation across four representative code-related tasks (bias instruction detection, malicious instruction detection, vulnerable code detection, and prompt injection detection) shows that BlueCodeAgent achieves significant gains over diverse baselines. In particular, for vulnerability detection tasks, BlueCodeAgent integrates dynamic analysis to effectively reduce false positives, a challenging problem as base models tend to be over-conservative. Overall, with GPT-4o as the base model, BlueCodeAgent achieves an average F1 score improvement of 14.7% across four tasks compared to directly prompting the model, attributed to its ability to summarize actionable constitutions and perform dynamic analysis. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/1mocat/BlueCodeAgent.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: ASTOR: Multi-Task Code Reinforcement Learning via Utility-Driven Coordination
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has proven effective at post-training LLMs for coding, yet deploying separate task-specific specialists incurs costs that scale with the number of tasks, motivating a unified multi-task RL (MTRL) approach. However, existing MTRL methods treat all coding tasks uniformly, relying on fixed data curricula under a shared optimization strategy, ultimately limiting the effectiveness of multi-task training. To address these limitations, we propose ASTOR, a multi-tASk code reinforcement learning framework via uTility-driven coORdination. Centered on task utility, a signal capturing each task learning potential and cross-task synergy, ASTOR comprises two coupled modules: 1) Hierarchical Utility-Routed Data Scheduling module hierarchically allocates training budget and prioritizes informative prompts, steering training toward the most valuable data and 2) Adaptive Utility-Calibrated Policy Optimization module dynamically scales per-task KL regularization, matching update constraints to each tasks current training state. Experiments on two widely-used LLMs across four representative coding tasks demonstrate that ASTOR consistently improves a single model across all tasks, outperforming the best task-specific specialist by 9.0%-9.5% and surpassing the strongest MTRL baseline by 7.5%-12.8%.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Program Bindings Inside Code Models
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Code language models complete, review, and repair programs without exposing the program structure encoded in their hidden states. In this paper, we test whether the hidden states of a code model can be described and edited using the information a compiler front end computes. For each token of a Python program, standard analyzers provide its position in the abstract syntax tree, its scope, its definition-use links, and its syntactic category. We fit a decomposition that expresses every hidden state of a frozen model as a sum of one term per token, each combining the token with this structural label, and we replace the model's own states with the decomposition at every layer while it predicts the output of a small program. If the model still answers correctly, the decomposition preserves the information the model uses. We apply this test to 14 open models, seven of them trained for code, and compare against a baseline decomposition of the same size built from token positions. The static-analysis decomposition preserves the model's answers better than the positional one in 10 of the 14 models, including six of the seven code models, and deleting the definition-use links from it removes most of that advantage on the two models tested. Editing the decomposition, for instance rebinding the argument of a call, makes StarCoder2-15B produce the answer of the edited program in 90 of 100 cases, compared with 19 for the positional baseline. The Qwen2.5 family is the exception on several measures. For most of the models tested, standard static analysis therefore provides both a description of what the hidden states encode about a program and a way to change it without retraining.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: RedCodeAgent: Automatic Red-teaming Agent against Diverse Code Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Code agents have gained widespread adoption due to their strong code generation capabilities and integration with code interpreters, enabling dynamic execution, debugging, and interactive programming capabilities. While these advancements have streamlined complex workflows, they have also introduced critical safety and security risks. Current static safety benchmarks and red-teaming tools are inadequate for identifying emerging real-world risky scenarios, as they fail to cover certain boundary conditions, such as the combined effects of different jailbreak tools. In this work, we propose RedCodeAgent, the first automated red-teaming agent designed to systematically uncover vulnerabilities in diverse code agents. With an adaptive memory module, RedCodeAgent can leverage existing jailbreak knowledge, dynamically select the most effective red-teaming tools and tool combinations in a tailored toolbox for a given input query, thus identifying vulnerabilities that might otherwise be overlooked. For reliable evaluation, we develop simulated sandbox environments to additionally evaluate the execution results of code agents, mitigating potential biases of LLM-based judges that only rely on static code. Through extensive evaluations across multiple state-of-the-art code agents, diverse risky scenarios, and various programming languages, RedCodeAgent consistently outperforms existing red-teaming methods, achieving higher attack success rates and lower rejection rates with high efficiency. We further validate RedCodeAgent on real-world code assistants, e.g., Cursor and Codeium, exposing previously unidentified security risks. By automating and optimizing red-teaming processes, RedCodeAgent enables scalable, adaptive, and effective safety assessments of code agents. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/1mocat/RedCodeAgent.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Soei: Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent for Multi-Agent AI Software Engineering
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI coding agents now do long, multi-step and multi-session software work with little supervision. When a developer comes back to that work, the useful question is not what the model said but what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished. We study this in three parts. First, we verify Agenttrail, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, against its source at commit e4ba2da: nine documented constants and mechanisms hold at file-and-line level, two event pipelines are never unified, and its Map service has an unauthenticated local mutation surface. Second, we run a prototype of our system on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes). With a blind-audited classifier (precision 83.3% and 96.7%) we estimate that 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete after editing had no proof in between. A 10-minute timing heuristic for session hand-offs recovers 6 of the 24 session pairs that content lineage links. 42% of sessions run longer than 24 hours, 48.1% of transcript bytes lie past a 2 MiB replay bound, and 1,326 records in 16 sessions contain credential-like strings. Third, we propose Soei (Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent): an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer that keeps a claim of completion apart from proof. On the same corpus the ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s, detects tampering and replays deterministically. We position the work against concurrent 2026 proposals and define autonomy levels with evidence gates and harness metrics baselined on our data.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Towards Functional Correctness of Code Models with Selective Generation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The hallucination of code generation models hinders their applicability to systems requiring higher safety standards. One critical bottleneck in addressing code hallucination is the difficulty of identifying the functional correctness of generated code, due to its unnatural form. We address this core bottleneck by automatically generating unit tests using dynamic code analysis tools, leveraging the \emph{executable nature} of code. Accordingly, we propose a \emph{selective code generator} that abstains from uncertain generations -- based on the functional correctness evaluated by generated unit tests -- to theoretically control the correctness among non-abstained answers, \ie the false discovery rate. Finally, we propose to use generated unit tests in evaluation as well as in learning for precise code evaluation, calling this paradigm \emph{FuzzEval}. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method along with the controllability of code hallucination and reasonable selection efficiency.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering (SE) tasks, driving the need for high-quality datasets for reliable training and evaluation. SWE-bench-style datasets (SWE datasets) are widely used to evaluate LLM-based coding agents on real-world software issues, where task clarity and test coverage directly affect whether instances are solvable and verifiable. However, quality issues persist in existing SWE datasets, and manual annotation is costly and labor-intensive, motivating LLM-based annotation. Existing approaches typically rely on static, overly general rubrics, limiting their ability to handle diverse and nuanced scenarios and often yielding high false positive rates. In contrast, human annotators draw on accumulated experience to make context-aware judgments. Inspired by this, we propose ExLabel, an LLM-based, self-evolving, experience-guided assistant for task clarity and test coverage assessment in SWE datasets. ExLabel maintains an evolving experience bank that distills cross-instance knowledge into stable yet adaptive judgment criteria and reuses relevant experience to guide the assessment of new instances. For systematic evaluation, we construct SWE-TQ, a new benchmark spanning eight programming languages, by cleaning human annotations from SWE-bench and Multi-SWE-bench. Experiments with three backbone LLMs show that ExLabel achieves the best F1 across all settings, with relative improvements of 44.2%/49.9% and 24.0%/18.4% over the best baseline for task clarity and test coverage assessment on the Python/Multilingual subsets, respectively. Moreover, a coding model fine-tuned on SWE-rebench data filtered by ExLabel resolves 66.2% of issues on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the model trained on data filtered by the best baseline by 14.5%.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: QSoftCore: A Conceptual Foundation for Quantum Software Engineering
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Quantum software engineering (QSE) requires understanding application requirements, quantum programs and algorithms, quantum computation paradigms, executions, and deployment. However, relevant quantum computing (QC) concepts are often defined across physical, mathematical, and paradigm-specific levels of abstraction, making it difficult for the QSE community and hence proposed methods to refer to them consistently. To this end, we present QSoftCore, a conceptual model that reorganizes established QC concepts from a software engineering perspective and connects quantum applications, computational problems, algorithms, configurations, programs, and paradigm-specific computation specifications with state evolution, execution results, and backends. Our assessment against QSE literature across key software engineering activities indicates that QSoftCore provides shared QC referents for quantum computations, executions, deployment configurations, backends, and measurement evidence across the QSE lifecycle.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Data-Efficient Unknown Attack Detection in IoT Networks Using Pretrained Language Models
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The rapid evolution of cyberattacks continues to drive the emergence of unknown (zero-day) threats, posing significant challenges for network intrusion detection systems in Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Existing machine learning and deep learning approaches typically rely on large labeled datasets, payload inspection, or closed-set classification, limiting their effectiveness under data scarcity, encrypted traffic, and distribution shifts. To address these limitations, we propose SiamXBERT, a data-efficient, open-set Siamese meta-learning framework built on a pretrained language model for unknown-attack detection. The framework constructs a dual-modality feature representation by integrating flow-level and packet-level information, enabling richer behavioral modeling while remaining compatible with encrypted traffic. The model learns similarity patterns for known benign and attack classes using 100 labeled samples per class. It flags traffic that does not sufficiently match any known class as potentially unknown, using a threshold set without unknown-attack data. We evaluate SiamXBERT on two IoT intrusion detection datasets against five state-of-the-art detection methods. When training and testing are performed on the same dataset at this labeling budget, SiamXBERT attains the highest unknown F1-score, exceeding the strongest competing method on each dataset by 84.8% and 37.4%; the improvement is statistically significant against all five methods on one dataset and against four of the five on the other. When a model trained on one dataset is tested on another, SiamXBERT transfers effectively in one direction but degrades in the reverse, reflecting the rejection behavior learned from the source traffic rather than the choice of threshold. These results highlight the practicality of SiamXBERT for data-efficient unknown attack detection in real-world IoT environments.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: GUITestScape: Towards Open-set Evaluation on Exploratory GUI Testing
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Exploratory GUI testing is a particularly demanding setting for MLLM agents: without predefined test scripts, an agent must autonomously navigate an application and discover defects through its own interaction. However, current evaluation falls short on two fronts. First, existing benchmarks focus almost exclusively on interaction defects, leaving display defects outside the evaluation frame. Second, evaluation protocols are bound to predefined defect annotations, collapsing the testing process into a single end-state judgment that conflates qualitatively distinct failure modes. To address these challenges, we present GUITestScape, an interactive benchmark covering 61 real-world Android applications and 508 preset defects spanning interaction and display types, and introduce GUIJudge, an open-set evaluator that decomposes an agent's testing trajectory into independently diagnosable capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that GUIJudge achieves reliable process-aware evaluation beyond predefined annotations, substantially outperforming all baselines. Benchmarking on GUITestScape further reveals that detection remains the critical bottleneck for existing models across both defect types, and that integrating GUIJudge's verifiers into existing agents significantly boosts their detection performance without retraining.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Benchmarking Coding Agents under Evolving Requirements
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Software development with coding agents often begins with a rough request that users refine after trying the implementation. Final correctness alone does not capture the repeated guidance this process requires. We introduce FeatureLoop, a benchmark of 61 human-reviewed tasks from 34 repositories across five primary programming languages and seven software forms. Each task follows one development goal in a persistent workspace through evolution feedback, which adds or clarifies requirements, and completion feedback, which reports failures of stated requirements. Cumulative executable checks track new behavior, repair, and preservation of earlier functionality. We evaluate 12 frontier models and find that the strongest completes 72.1% of tasks with both feedback types. Across models, however, only 15.4% of observed failed stages recover within two corrective revisions. Further analysis reveals incomplete repairs, regressions, and model-specific differences in feedback use and token efficiency, identifying obstacles to reliable, low-intervention development.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Broken on Arrival: Non-Functional Quantized LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Developers download quantized large language models (LLMs) from public registries to run them locally. None of the registries we examined documented functional testing of their files. We tested all 305 eligible code-capable GGUF tags (the llama.cpp format) across 15 model lines in the official Ollama library, plus 22 popular Hugging Face community files. A 15-task code screen identified suspects, which we retested on all 164 HumanEval+ tasks. Seven official tags (2.3%) solved at most six of them. All were low-bit quantizations of models with at most four billion parameters. We rebuilt five suspect files from the original weights. All five registry files matched our uncalibrated rebuilds tensor for tensor, so none was corrupted. Exact reproducibility did not imply function. With the weights, toolchain and tensor mix held fixed, adding an importance matrix raised Qwen2.5-Coder-3B scores at three quantization levels from zero to 76-113 of 164 tasks. The same uncalibrated recipe left the smaller Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B functional, showing that the recipe alone does not predict failure. None of 66 sampled tags that passed the screen was non-functional. We release the audit data and the quantcheck tool and recommend screening low-bit tags before publication, then calibrating or withholding failures.

V, RQ2): a template test on the same hardware shows the two deepseek-coder-6.7B community files fail for lack of a chat template, not by backend; release v3.4 adds the test. All other results unchanged. Code and data: https://github.com/aditi-p31/quantcheck (release v3.4)

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Omission-Safe Conditional Contracts for Evidence-Closed CI Qualification
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Continuous-integration evidence is conditional: a workflow determines which jobs should run, while an archive records which jobs remain observable. Reconstructing requirements from those observations lets an omission erase its own obligation. We present a qualification method that compiles a pinned workflow into conditional job requirements independently of target presence, retains a fixed capture inventory, and checks source-complete derivation certificates with a separate implementation. For a fixed source, context, scope and binding universe, with sound obligations and applicability judgments that preserve established truth under information extension, withdrawing observation facts cannot create authorization. The implementation handles static matrices, dependency guards and bounded pinned reusable workflows, preserving unknown applicability and separating tolerated outcomes from evidence coverage. Both implementations match the 45 hand-specified authorization controls, reject 180 source-certificate attacks, and exhibit no authorization gain over 704 distinct proper development erasures. An explicitly witnessed 12-job platform run qualifies in both implementations; all 4,095 proper payload-subset erasures block authorization. A frozen collection spans 240 runs in eight workflow families across six projects. All 160 evaluation source certificates independently validate, but unavailable historical execution-source identities leave actual qualification open. Initial gate diagnoses agree on 155/160 runs; a preserved unknown-propagation repair yields 160/160 agreement in a retrospective rerun. The study establishes bounded source extraction and omission resistance, rather than natural-fault prevalence or producer authenticity.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: PyReprism: A Shared Lexical Foundation for Polyglot Code Analysis
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Empirical studies of polyglot repositories apply the same analyses to every language of a corpus, such as separating code from comments, computing metrics, normalizing identifiers, and screening for duplicated code. Assembling them from specialized tools introduces differences in language coverage, measurement conventions, and workflows. We present PYREPRISM, an open-source Python library and command-line tool that separates language-specific lexical processing from reusable analyses: each language declares its lexical surface, which yields a lossless stream of typed tokens, and every analysis is implemented once on that stream. Across 187 built-in languages, language-specific declarations have a median length of 16 lines, and no language overrides a shared analysis. Against a reference parser, comment and string classification reach F1 scores of 0.994 and 0.958 on 1,412 files in 12 languages that were never used to develop the tokenizer. In a study of a polyglot repository, one tool replaces three; with matched inputs and analysis operations, it takes 2.9s instead of 8.7s on one core. We also characterize where lexical analysis falls short, in complexity estimation and clone screening. Tool: https://github.com/unlv-evol/PyReprism Video: https://youtu.be/IXc-NP5t4GU
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, Submitted to SANER 2027 Tool Demo Track

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Confident Learning-based Network for Detecting Bug-Inducing Commits on SZZ with Noisy Labels
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The Just-In-Time (JIT) defect prediction model serves as a critical tool for ensuring the quality of software development and enhancing software performance. It assists development teams in promptly identifying and addressing potential issues by predicting whether code submissions may introduce defects. However, due to the existence of data noise and insufficient semantic connections in real-world scenarios, existing approaches face challenges in accurately identifying the code commits that introduce defects and capturing the potential semantic relationships. To address these challenges, we propose the BIC- Hunter(Bug-Inducing Commits Hunter) model, which mitigates data noise and improves semantic understanding, thereby enhancing the accuracy of bug-inducing commit identification. BIC - Hunter model consists of two components: a data denoising component and a semantic relationship capturing component. Specifically, the data denoising component addresses the challenges posed by inaccurate annotations and inconsistencies in real-world data, enhancing the reliability of training data and improving overall model robustness. The semantic relation- ship capturing component constructs homogeneous graphs and applies graph convolutional networks to facilitate a more comprehensive analysis of code context, enabling the identification of defects caused by code commits and enhancing the confidence in pinpointing their root causes. Experimental studies on a large-scale dataset integrated from three open-source datasets show that BIC- Hunter exhibits outstanding performance. BIC- Hunter outperforms the state-of-the-art by 6.16%, 7.13%, and 5.53% on Recall@1, Recall@2, and Recall@3, respectively, while the MFR index increases by 8.43% to 32.82%. These results demonstrate the superior capability of our method in identifying bug-inducing commits.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Rebuild Dossier: Mechanically-Enforced Specs for Agentic App Rebuilds, and What Model-Tier Failures Reveal
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
An AI agent's rebuild is only as good as the process that produced it. Prior work found that once a model is strong enough, a multi-agent rebuild pipeline loses to the simplest approach: giving the model the original code and one instruction (AgentModernize). We present rebuild-dossier, an open-source tool that locks an application's real interface - its exact inputs and outputs - before any code is written, then enforces one-test-at-a-time building through automated checks, not written instructions alone.
  Three results shape this evaluation, with differing amounts of evidence. First, in a small comparison, the compliant agent failed a held-back test while the rule-breaking agent passed everything - proof that a passing suite doesn't certify correctness when tests can be gamed. Second, we tested whether this beats simply giving the weaker model the source and one instruction: tied on a small app, but lost outright on a larger one where the automated check wasn't even running - pointing to the check mechanism, not interface-locking, which held up separately. Third, every claim here is checked at three levels - the agent's own report, an automated log, and the actual files produced - catching real errors, including a bug in our own logging code, that a single level would have missed.
  These risks reproduce on a different model and toolchain: a stronger model followed our process three times running, something the weaker model never managed. The tool is public, MIT licensed, and reproduces end to end against our own applications.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Do Open-Source Video Ad Clients Follow VAST 4.3? An Empirical Study of Player Conformance
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Context. Video ads reach streaming and connected-TV apps through VAST documents, and companies count ads from the HTTP requests the player's client library sends. A tracking error can leave playback intact and surface later as disagreeing counts.
  Objective. To measure how far open-source VAST clients meet the player duties of VAST 4.3, whether verdicts depend on the runtime, what generated inputs add, and when deviations were introduced.
  Method. A catalog of 108 requirements was extracted from the specification. Six open-source clients in eight configurations ran against 69 crafted test vectors and the IAB's sample tags, under Node.js and in five browsers on three engines, with every request recorded. Grids, fuzzing and a sweep over 36 releases extend the catalog; Google's closed IMA SDK is a comparison.
  Results. The open-source clients have 78 findings and 3 to 21 must-level deviations per configuration. None of the tested open-source clients that follow redirect (Wrapper) chains fills the required macros in a Wrapper's request; the archived IMA 3.794.0 configuration tested does. One library's timeout throws an exception no caller can catch, ending a Node.js process. In a pod (ads played back to back), one player credits a finishing ad's completion to the next ad, fixed in release 5.3.0. A library can conform under jsdom and deviate in every tested Chrome- and Safari-family browser.
  Conclusions. The tested clients diverge on the duties other companies use to count and diagnose ads. A shared conformance suite run in real browsers could expose most graded deviations; the harness and vectors are released.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 51 pages, 20 tables, 3 figures. Harness, test vectors and results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23581408

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Superintelligent Software Engineering: Governance That Scales with Capability
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Software agents are being trained to exceed human engineers; we argue that capability alone does not produce better software engineering. We define superintelligent software engineering as the discipline of building and evolving software with agents whose capability exceeds that of human engineers, in which governance (gates, contracts, decisions and decay control) scales with capability. The argument rests on three claims. First, correctness in a project rests on decisions and contracts that the code does not carry. Second, knowledge decays. Third, once an agent outpaces its reviewers, reading catches a shrinking share of the changes built on stale knowledge. A simple model shows that, past a fixed review capacity, escaping changes grow linearly with throughput while the share that reading catches falls toward zero; governance can lower the slope, capability alone cannot. An exploratory snapshot of 452 of the most-starred public GitHub repositories finds a root-level or .github agent context file in 48.67% (95% confidence interval 44.1 to 53.3); in the median file that names repository paths, 9.5% to 22% of those paths do not resolve, depending on how a reference is read. We then present OSTEON, a discipline for the regime, archived on Zenodo under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23436020 as a plugin for Claude Code. In OSTEON, each project gets a governed knowledge repository of decisions and contracts, every change is checked mechanically against it, and the knowledge itself is checked for decay at every session start; planning is gated, and sessions record what they learn without writing rules. We report no measured effect of OSTEON, mark claims about its mechanisms as opinion and the author's practice heuristics as design rationale, and state the questions that would falsify the thesis.

This version updates citations, corrects a cost figure, marks opinion sentences and clarifies where capability enters the model. Collection scripts and dataset are provided as ancillary files. The OSTEON artifact is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23436020 and registrations for the empirical follow-up are at https://osf.io/s4w2t and https://osf.io/8scgm

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Measuring Delivery Consistency in Practice: A DORA Extension from a Multi-Platform Release Setting
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) framework is the most widely adopted measurement system for performance measurement across engineering teams. However, every DORA metric is a first-moment statistic or a simple ratio, which limits the potential insights into engineering process. For example, metrics like Deployment Frequency do not capture the distributional shape of deployment timing, so teams with identical measures can deploy on a metronomic cadence or in undesirably erratic bursts. We have been developing and piloting Delivery Consistency (DC), a bounded second-moment measure of cadence regularity derived from the coefficient of variation of inter-release intervals. In conjunction with other DORA concepts, we integrated DC into the Delivery Health Matrix, an eight-archetype diagnostic that maps joint readings to differentiated interventions. We report an experience evaluation on a four-platform software delivery group using 120 weeks of data extracted from our Jira, GitHub, and Firebase records. DC allowed us to distinguish platforms with identical DORA tier placements but different cadence regularity, and the Matrix summarized the readings into an archetype that pointed at a shared organization or procedural constraint.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Context-Specific Instruction: A Longitudinal Study on Debugging Skill Acquisition and Retention for Novice Programmers
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Bug localization is a critical skill, yet novices often lack systematic approaches. Prior work tested abstract guidelines and general concrete steps; the impact of context-specific instruction is unclear. We ran an eight-week longitudinal study with four conditions: no instruction (G1), abstract guidelines (G2), concrete steps (G3), and our context-specific instruction that pairs concrete bug-localization steps with problem-specific details (G4). Forty-four undergraduates participated; 41 completed all five sessions (S1-S5). Each session included 2-3 debugging tasks to identify the minimal code element containing a seeded logical fault. We measured correctness (binary), time to completion, self-perceived scores (stress, difficulty, satisfaction, and strategy adherence). G4 achieved higher correctness and shorter time to completion: it reached 80% correctness after one session (vs. 20-44% for other groups) and maintained 80% after three weeks, outperforming all groups (p < 0.05); its time to completion stabilized at 13-15 minutes in S1, whereas other groups took 2-3 sessions to stabilize at 22-27 minutes. Qualitative responses showed lower stress and higher satisfaction in G4, with participants internalizing strategies via contextual examples. We conclude that context-specific instruction yields faster skill acquisition and stronger retention than abstract guidelines or context-agnostic steps. Even 1-2 sessions produced significant gains, while extended practice optimized and stabilized performance. Integrating contextual examples with abstract principles may bridge theory-practice gaps in bug-localization education and provide a more equitable path for novices.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: An Empirical Study of Gas Optimization Practices in Solidity Smart Contracts
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: In the Ethereum ecosystem, smart contract execution is governed by a gas model where every computational operation incurs a direct economic cost. Consequently, gas efficiency is a critical requirement for the economic sustainability and widespread adoption of decentralized applications. Despite the importance of cost-effective development, there remains a significant gap between theoretical optimization patterns and the actual practices applied by developers in real-world projects. This paper presents an empirical study investigating gas optimization practices in open-source Solidity repositories created on GitHub between 2018 and 2025. Adopting a Mining Software Repositories approach, we analyzed a dataset of gas-related commits identified through a multi-stage pipeline involving NLP-based filtering and manual qualitative inspection. Based on the analysis of 400 representative commits, we derive an empirical taxonomy of gas optimization strategies consisting of 8 macro-categories and 36 subcategories. Our findings reveal that optimization efforts span multiple levels of abstraction, from low-level arithmetic refinements and bytecode-size reductions to broader architectural changes such as logic internalization and external call reduction. Furthermore, we observe that developers often manage complex trade-offs between execution frequency, safety checks, and computational costs, highlighting that effective optimization is inherently context-dependent. This study provides a practical knowledge base for the design of future developer support tools and advances the understanding of cost-aware software engineering in the blockchain domain.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: From GPU to TPU with Coding Agents: What Works, What Fails, and What It Costs?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: A coding agent can migrate a machine learning workload, report success, and still change how the model trains. Rising compute costs, limited accelerator capacity, and vendor dependence are pushing organizations toward alternatives to graphics processing units (GPUs); a key question is whether agent-generated migrations to tensor processing units (TPUs) can be trusted and at what cost. We build a dataset of 148 PyTorch ML research projects and use Claude Code to migrate ten of them from NVIDIA GPUs to Google Cloud TPUs. We independently assess whether each migration runs, preserves numerical behavior, executes on the intended hardware, maintains the project's goal, and delivers acceptable performance. We also examine failures, human effort, and costs. Eight projects meet our project-goal criterion, and migrations require 2.4 human interventions on average. Of 70 execution attempts, 53 fail (76%), and 26 of these failures (49%) raise no error. The most frequent cause is repeated compilation and other execution inefficiencies, while interactions with third-party libraries can silently change the computation: in one four-chip migration, the agent reports success despite a change in gradient clipping that reduces accuracy from 86.53% to 84.89%. Execution costs vary widely: in one workload, TorchTPU, a PyTorch execution backend for TPUs, trains 1.86 times faster and 25% cheaper per run than the GPU. For practitioners, these findings motivate independent reference runs, verification under the intended hardware configuration, and workload-specific acceptance and stopping criteria that account for both computational and human costs.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: RiskyPy: Toward Model-Calibrated Prompt Generation for Joint Security and Functionality Evaluation of LLM-Generated Code
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Evaluating approaches that improve the security of LLM code generation requires datasets that jointly assess security and functionality and remain adapted to the capabilities of the models being studied. However, existing benchmarks are costly to produce and are generally not calibrated to a chosen range of model capabilities. We introduce RiskyPy, an automated pipeline that generates security-oriented code-generation datasets calibrated to model proficiency using functionality and vulnerability canaries. We instantiate RiskyPy for Python using domains covering 18 CWEs from the 2025 CWE Top 25, producing 101 prompts. Experiments on Qwen3-4B and Seed-Coder-8B show that the generated tasks remain functionally accessible, with 57-72% of prompts yielding functional code, while only 5-10% of generations are free of Bandit findings, leaving room for joint evaluation of security and functionality of security improvement approaches.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to automate vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly, the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the harness: the code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static, improvements on one dataset or model may not transfer to others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each iteration, it searches over the history of prior harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for various architectures. A validation set (202 pairs) is used for optimization, while an unseen dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to others. We show that harnesses optimized with one model transfer to another, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Differentially Private Covariate Balancing Causal Inference
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Differential privacy is the leading mathematical framework for privacy protection, providing a probabilistic guarantee that safeguards individuals' private information when publishing statistics from a dataset. This guarantee is achieved by applying a randomized algorithm to the original data, which introduces unique challenges in data analysis by distorting inherent patterns. In particular, causal inference using observational data while preserving privacy is challenging because it requires a good covariate balance between treatment groups, but checking the covariate balance is challenging when privacy is a primary concern because releasing any statistic (e.g., t-statistic) for the balance check compromises privacy. Additionally, the performance of the privatized estimator critically depends on the choice of differential privacy mechanisms, and it remains unexplored how privacy-protecting causal inference could be conducted with observational data. In this article, we present a differentially private two-stage covariate balancing weighting estimator to infer causal effects from observational data. Our algorithm produces both point and interval estimators with statistical guarantees, such as covariate balance, rate optimality, and oracle budget allocation, under a given privacy budget.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 47 pages

Security & Program Analysis.title: Difficulty Calibration Across Time for Membership Inference in Diffusion Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Modern diffusion models are trained on massive datasets that often include copyrighted or private images. Membership inference attacks (MIAs) address this by testing whether a given image was in a model's training set. The standard approach scores an image by its reconstruction loss and flags low-loss images as members. This often fails because some images are simply easier to reconstruct than others, so a simple unseen image can score a lower loss than a complex training image. Difficulty calibration separates memorization from how difficult an image is to begin with. We show how to calibrate along two axes of time: training time and diffusion time. First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC), which compares a fine-tuned model's loss against an earlier checkpoint. This cleanly isolates newly memorized data and gives near-perfect auditing, even without text captions. Since earlier checkpoints are not always available, we next present Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC), which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. Our key observation is that an image's difficulty persists across noise levels, whereas memorization is localized in time. By comparing the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps from the same model, TSC attenuates image difficulty using the model's own trajectory. Empirically, our methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin, and unlike most existing attacks, generalize across different model parameterizations such as $x$-, $v$-, and $ε$-prediction models. Code is available at https://github.com/MichaelJoseph777/TSC.

Security & Program Analysis.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
Security & Program Analysis.summary: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Code: https://github.com/facebookresearch/textseal

Security & Program Analysis.title: Power Adjusting Games Under Block-Dependent Pool Payout Schemes
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Advanced power adjusting block withholding attacks such as PAW and T-PAW have been analyzed so far under a global-reset version of the proportional scheme (GRP), which is rarely used in practice. In this paper, we analyze T-PAW, which contains FAW and PAW as special cases, under the block-dependent payout schemes deployed in practice: Pay-Per-Last-N-Shares (PPLNS), round-based Proportional (PROP) and exponential-decay (EXP). We derive the revenue ratios analytically, by renewal arguments for PPLNS and through the stationary carry process of an open round for PROP and EXP. We further introduce Power Adjusting Hopping (PAH), where an adversary of any size adjusts its power allocation towards the pool according to the blockwork age of the round without withholding any block, and derive its revenue ratios under PROP and EXP. We show that GRP misestimates the T-PAW gain in a scheme-dependent direction: it overstates the gain under PROP up to an order of magnitude and understates it under EXP for the original slush decay rate. PROP is highly vulnerable to PAH, while EXP faces a trade-off: a slow decay invites PAH and a fast decay invites T-PAW. PPLNS is the least vulnerable scheme: it is immune to PAH and it mitigates, but does not eliminate, T-PAW. All analytical results are verified by Monte Carlo simulations.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Privacy and Security Risks of Edge LLM Optimization
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Edge deployment of Large Language Models requires optimization techniques that reduce memory, computation, and energy costs. However, preserving task performance does not necessarily preserve security. We argue that optimization is an information transformation that can alter representations, decision pathways, and trust boundaries, creating security drift and optimization-induced attack surfaces.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost.
  In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography.
  In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.
  RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Understanding and Enhancing Backdoor Persistency in LLM Agent Post-Training
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Developers can build LLM agents by adapting third-party models through benign post-training. We study a supply-chain threat in which an attacker supplies a model with a backdoor: hidden behavior that produces malicious outputs when a particular input pattern appears. Focusing on software-engineering agents, we ask whether such backdoors survive the developer's supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and subsequent task-level reinforcement learning (RL). We observe that benign SFT substantially reduces attack success, but subsequent RL often preserves the residual behavior and sometimes even increases attack success. Our analysis of backdoor erosion during SFT identifies two factors that may favor survival: initial backdoor strength and gradient compatibility with benign training. These factors motivate PersistBD, which refines an already-backdoored model before release to improve its persistency through the benign post-training process. On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, PersistBD raises attack success from 20% to 74% after SFT and from 20% to 76% after SFT-RL, while maintaining comparable benign task performance. Together, our results show that backdoors can remain active through benign post-training and that adversaries can deliberately increase their persistence. This highlights a supply-chain risk for AI developers and motivates stronger techniques for detecting and mitigating inherited backdoors when adapting third-party models into agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/uiuc-kang-lab/PersistBD.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: EMNLP 2026 Findings

Security & Program Analysis.title: RecHash: Segmented Hash-Entangled Chains for Stateful Sequential Authentication
Security & Program Analysis.summary: RecHash is a stateful sequential authentication construction based on paired hash-chain openings and an authenticated record history. It develops the decreasing position relation of the 2019 hash-entangled construction, whose exact integer normalization yields a two-coordinate constant-sum antichain. Direct proportional reuse is constrained by integer capacity and multiplicative contraction. The main construction instead assigns each record to a predetermined chain segment, with complementary positions encoding each digest block. All digests fit every scheduled slot, independently of preceding messages. For an $\ell$-bit digest distributed over $k$ equal-length chain pairs, balanced allocation gives $\lfloor L/(2^{\lceil\ell/k\rceil}+1)\rfloor$ slots. A 256-bit digest, 32 pairs, and length 65535 provide 254 application records followed by a renewal certificate, with 2048 bytes of openings per record for 256-bit chain outputs. We give a complete segmented state transition, a worked trace, exact allocation and resource results, and a renewal-free security-composition theorem conditional on authenticated history and an adaptive one-step guarantee. The analysis relates the construction to constant-sum encodings and standardized hash-based signatures; a concrete post-quantum reduction and security across renewal remain open.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 23 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables

Security & Program Analysis.title: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Traffic cameras support useful analysis, but their outputs can reveal private information. Replacing images with text reduces direct visual exposure. It does not place a formal bound on disclosure. The published reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework refines scene descriptions through relevance, coverage, and brevity rewards. It does not account for repeated releases under a fixed privacy budget. This paper proposes budgeted semantic release as an extension of that framework. Four scene experts first process isolated video chunks. Their outputs are mapped to a fixed, bounded semantic schema. A reinforcement learning controller selects which expert summaries to release and how much privacy budget to spend. The controller uses public task requests and previous private releases. A separate privacy filter enforces the total budget. Calibrated noise is added before the summaries are converted to text. Under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the complete release transcript satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound. The design also supports reuse of previous summaries without new disclosure. An evaluation protocol covers traffic utility, privacy attacks, release freshness, and computational cost. Illustrative tables show the intended reporting format. They do not establish empirical gains. The proposed contribution is a task-aware release interface with auditable privacy accounting for repeated traffic descriptions.

Security & Program Analysis.title: WAAA! Web Adversaries Against Web Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into web browsers to create agentic browsing systems that execute actions on behalf of the user. Prior work considering the security of agentic browsers focuses on indirect prompt-injection attacks. However, by failing to consider traditional web attacks, previous agentic browser threat models have a blind spot to web social engineering attacks originally designed to trick humans. In this paper, we propose the first web-focused threat model for agentic browsers and use it to derive a taxonomy of 20 attacks across both the web and LLM space, and implement 18 of the attacks.
